newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot power up as weather boosts demand.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot power up as weather boosts demand.

text.p: Western U.S. spot power prices moved higher amid strong demand and cooler temperatures, market sources said Wednesday.
"Prices seemed to be strengthening as the morning wore off," said one dealer.
Northwest traders said cooler nighttime temperatures were serving to tighten power supplies.
But a northern California utility trader said loads for his service territory were relatively steady.
Sources said Bonneville Power Administration's (BPA) decision to raise firm peak prices for Thursday by $3.00 per meagwatt hour (MWh) had a big influence on the spot market.
BPA offered up to 300 MW of peak power at $16.00 per MWh for Northwest deliveries and $17.00 for California-Oregon border (COB).
Maintenance-related capacity cuts on the Pacific Intertie helped tighten the Southwest power market, sources said.
Traders also cited unplanned, albeit short-term, outages at several coal-fired plants as helping to tighten the market.
The 790 megawatt (MW) Mohave plant in Nevada was expected to be back on-line late Wednesday night after entering start-up mode early Wednesday.
The 750 MW Navajo plant in Arizona was also said to be back up after being shut Friday for unplanned repairs.
The 415 MW Hunter plant in Oregon was said to have tripped off Tuesday, but no official information was available on the plant's status.
Thursday firm, peak electricity at the California-Oregon border (COB) was quoted at $13.00-14.00 per megawatt hour (MWh), compared with $11.50-12.50 for Wednesday.
Firm, peak power at Mid-Columbia (Mid-C) was at $12.50-13.50, while off-peak was at $6.00-7.00.
Firm, peak Palo Verde (PV) electricity was at $13.50-$14.50, while off-peak was quoted at $7.00-8.00.
Next-day firm, peak power at Four Corners was quoted at $13.00-14.00, while off-peak was at $7.00-8.00.
